title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
hook: Krishna sits alone by the Yamuna, and the god of the poem admits he let her walk away
carry: God is the one who misses

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and Radha slipping away from the spring dance into a bower of vines, still remembering him.

Krishna is sitting by the river Yamuna, alone, and he is not doing well. A little while ago he was at the center of a spring dance in the forest, everyone around him. Then he noticed someone missing. Radha had seen him there, surrounded, and had quietly gone. He left the dance and searched the thickets and the vine bowers. Nothing. Now he has sat down on the bank, and Jayadeva lets us listen while he talks to himself. It isn't the speech a listener might expect from a god.
screen: `A DANCE, AND SOMEONE MISSING.` → `HE SEARCHES THE THICKETS.` → `ALONE ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: Here is his song, in paraphrase. She saw me surrounded by the other women, and she walked away. I didn't stop her. I was afraid, because I knew I was in the wrong. Then the refrain, again and again: Hari, Hari, through my own carelessness she has gone, angry, it seems. What will she do now? What will she say to me, after I've been away so long? What good is wealth, or people, or a home, without her? He sees her face in his mind, the eyebrows drawn together in anger, and speaks to her as if she were there: forgive me, I won't do it again, let me see you. This is the Lord of the poem, the one the opening hymn praised in every one of his descents into the world. And here he sits, admitting a mistake. How do devotees hold this? In Vaishnava traditions, one answer is the word lila, play. The divine takes on a lover's part fully, faults and all, so that love can be shown in its whole range: delight, hurt, regret, longing. It's easy to picture bhakti running one way, the soul reaching up toward God. Here it runs the other way too. God is the one who misses, rehearsing an apology by the river. And Jayadeva closes his songs by naming himself, offering what he has sung. So even in Krishna's lament there's a third voice in the room, quietly saying: I made this as an offering.
screen: `I DIDN'T STOP HER. I WAS AFRAID.` · `WHAT WILL SHE SAY TO ME?` · `LILA: LOVE IN ITS WHOLE RANGE.` · `GOD IS THE ONE WHO MISSES.` · then, large: `HARI, HARI, SHE HAS GONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've let walk away without a word: a friend you stopped calling, a small hurt you saw and didn't answer. Don't fix anything; just sit on the riverbank with it, the way Krishna does in the poem, and let yourself see their face. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply stay with the memory, and breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda it runs both ways: today, the one who longs is Krishna.
Your line: God is the one who misses. In this poem, the longing runs both ways. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Singers in Vaishnava communities perform the Gita Govinda's songs in temples and in concert, often one song at a time, and dancers in classical forms such as Odissi act out scenes like Krishna's lament by the river.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: lila, play. Vaishnava traditions use it for the divine taking part in the world freely, as in Krishna's love story.

chat.says: Why would a poem show Krishna, a god, sitting alone and upset by a river?
options: Because he let Radha walk away, admits it was his fault, and misses her.
Because Radha cursed him to lose his powers, and he's waiting for it to lift.
Because he's angry with Radha for leaving the dance without asking him.
chat.meaning: Jayadeva shows Krishna searching for Radha and admitting his fault. In this scene bhakti runs both ways: God is the one who misses.
